gr26-077.title: Inception
gr26-077.syn: A specialist in entering dreams attempts to plant an idea in a target's subconscious while confronting his own guilt and memories.
gr26-077.bio: Christopher Nolan was born in London on 30 July 1970 to an American mother and a British father. His company Syncopy, run with wife Emma Thomas, produced Inception; he went on to make Interstellar, Dunkirk, Tenet and Oppenheimer, shooting several films on IMAX and 70mm film.
highlights: About ten years in the making; first conceived as a horror film.
Eight Oscar nominations and four wins: Cinematography, Sound Editing, Sound Mixing and Visual Effects.
Different colour palettes mark dream layers, with many practical sets.
Hans Zimmer's score, with its signature low brass blast.
gr26-077.st:
Nolan has said the story took about ten years to crack: according to the Los Angeles Times he had the idea at sixteen and wrote a first draft around 2002, originally as a horror film, and began working on it in earnest only after The Dark Knight. Many ideas about Cobb came from Leonardo DiCaprio. The budget was about $160 million and the working title was Oliver's Arrow.

Cinematographer Wally Pfister used different colour palettes for each dream layer; he and Nolan considered a 3D conversion but dropped it because of the story's complexity. Hans Zimmer's score is about sixty percent electronic, and its low brass blast became the film's signature. It premiered in London on 8 July 2010, opened on 16 July and grossed over $800 million worldwide.

Inception received eight Oscar nominations (including Best Picture and Original Screenplay) and won four: Cinematography, Sound Editing, Sound Mixing and Visual Effects.
gr26-077.editorial: The layered dream structure takes concentration, but the emotional line is simple: a man weighed by guilt wants to go home. The ending's spinning top need not have an answer; you can leave the cinema with the question.
gr26-077.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Violence or injury; Death and bereavement; Psychological distress or uncertainty. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-078.title: Ground Floor
gr26-078.syn: A man investigates mould in his apartment and becomes trapped in a building-wide tangle of evasion, secrecy and competing interests.
gr26-078.bio: Gábor Reisz was born in Budapest on 19 January 1980 and studied film theory and history at Eötvös Loránd University. His Explanation for Everything (2023) won the Orizzonti prize for Best Film in Venice, and he returned as a jury member the following year. Ground Floor (Földszint) is his fourth feature, premiering in the Venice Spotlight section in 2026, co-written with Éva Schulze as a Hungarian-Italian co-production.
highlights: World premiere in Venice Spotlight; the director's previous film Explanation for Everything won the Orizzonti prize for Best Film.
A patch of black mould unravels a whole building's evasions, snitching and vested interests.
A grotesque comedy; critics read the apartment block as a metaphor for Hungarian society.
He learns he will be a father on the day he finds the mould: private life and social pressure arrive together.
gr26-078.st:
The film had its world premiere in the Venice Spotlight section of the 83rd Venice Film Festival in 2026. Its hero Kristóf (Ádám Tompa) is a former painter now working as a bank archivist; on the same day he learns he will become a father he discovers black mould spreading on the wall of his ground-floor flat. He sets out to trace where the water comes from and moves through the whole building: snitching superintendents, corrupt building managers, a drunken mould specialist. A small repair becomes a Kafkaesque journey.

Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera describes it as a grotesque comedy that can be read as a coded allegory of the previous regime; Cineuropa calls the mould a clear metaphor for Orbán-era Hungary. It is produced by Proton Cinema (Juli Berkes) with Italian producer Andrea Romeo.

His previous film, Explanation for Everything, won the Orizzonti prize in 2023 and likewise placed an individual's predicament inside a larger social mood.
gr26-078.editorial: Suited to viewers who like absurdist comedy with some social satire. Notice how neighbours on each floor dodge the same problem in different ways, and how Kristóf, who only wants the wall fixed, is gradually pulled in.
gr26-078.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Unsafe housing; Sexual or reproductive themes; Neighbour conflict. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-079.title: Visitation
gr26-079.syn: A lakeside house near Berlin witnesses successive residents, persecution, exile, division and reunification over a turbulent century.
gr26-079.bio: Volker Schlöndorff was born in Wiesbaden on 31 March 1939 and is a leading figure of New German Cinema. His first feature, Young Törless (1966), won the FIPRESCI Prize at Cannes, and The Tin Drum (1979) won the Palme d'Or. Visitation is his 28th film, shown in Cannes Première in 2026 when he was 87.
highlights: Schlöndorff's 28th film, shown in Cannes Première.
One lakeside house witnesses the Nazi era, war and exile, division and reunification.
Shot in Einstein's holiday home, with the crew working there for a full year.
Adapted from Jenny Erpenbeck's novel, with Martina Gedeck, Lars Eidinger and Susanne Wolff.
gr26-079.st:
The film is adapted from Jenny Erpenbeck's novel Heimsuchung (English edition 2010); Schlöndorff wrote the script himself and calls it a free adaptation. It centres on a house by a lake near Berlin where several families live in turn: from the Nazi era, war and exile, through the division of Germany to the fall of the Berlin Wall, the house barely changes while its people keep losing, searching and redefining what home means.

In Cannes' official interview the director says the house is not a set but Albert Einstein's holiday home, which he had to flee when the Nazis came to power; a young Bauhaus architect had designed it. The house was in fact some 40 kilometres from the lake, so the film puts it beside the water. The crew could come and go for a whole year, and the actors and children grew accustomed to it.

The cast includes Martina Gedeck, Lars Eidinger, Susanne Wolff and Ulrich Matthes, with cinematography by Axel Schneppat. Cineuropa calls it meticulously crafted and tenderly intimate, a historical epic spanning nearly a century; RogerEbert.com feels the wide scope makes some events plod while others lose clarity. It opened in Germany on 15 October 2026.
gr26-079.editorial: The film spans a long time with many characters, so watch the house itself first: how its walls, windows and lake are passed to new owners across the decades. If you like literary adaptations or modern German history, it is easier to enter.
warnings: War, conflict or threat of war
gr26-079.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Nazi-era persecution and its aftermath; War, conflict or threat of war; Migration or displacement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-080.title: Viva Carmen!
gr26-080.syn: Street children in Seville try to save the spirited Carmen from a tragic fate foretold by a prophecy.
gr26-080.bio: Sébastien Laudenbach is a French animation director. The Girl Without Hands (2016) was his first animated feature; Chicken for Linda!, co-directed with Chiara Malta (2023), won the Cristal at Annecy and the César for Best Animated Film. Viva Carmen is his third animated feature; it premiered in Directors' Fortnight at Cannes in 2026, then competed at Annecy and played the Centrepiece section at TIFF.
highlights: Premiered in Directors' Fortnight, then competed at Annecy and played the Centrepiece section at TIFF.
Retells Carmen through the street children of the opera's opening chorus.
Vividly coloured, like a handmade storybook; most of the opera's music is replaced by a new score.
Music by Amine Bouhafa and flamenco guitarist Isabelle Laudenbach.
gr26-080.st:
The film is adapted from Bizet's opera Carmen (itself based on Mérimée's novella), from an original idea by producer Pierre-Henri Léon and the director, with a screenplay by Santiago Otheguy and Laudenbach. It is set in Seville in 1820: Salvador, young assistant to the knife grinder Antonio, meets the captivating, free-spirited Carmen. Antonio can glimpse the future in sharpened blades and foresees that she will die at the hands of the soldier José. Salvador and a band of street kids led by Belén decide to defy fate and save her. Laudenbach takes the children's chorus that opens the opera as his entry point and retells the story through the street kids' eyes.

He told Variety in Cannes that he wanted to show a real woman rather than an icon: her priority is not love but freedom, and she is willing to pay the ultimate price for it. The film trims most of the opera's music, with a new score by Amine Bouhafa and the director's sister, flamenco guitarist Isabelle Laudenbach; Variety says the visuals do the singing.

Produced by Folivari, it was later completed in a Spanish-language version with a new song by singer Silvia Pérez Cruz, and opens in France on 16 December 2026.
gr26-080.editorial: No need to know the opera: it enters through the children, and Carmen is a woman who values freedom above love. Come for the hand-drawn animation and colour.
gr26-080.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Crime, threat or interpersonal conflict; Death and bereavement. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-081.title: Princess Peacock
gr26-081.syn: A prince seeks his beloved peacock princess after court intrigue forces them apart, facing trials of courage and loyalty.
gr26-081.bio: Jin Xi, from Tianjin, began studying painting in 1936, joined the Eighth Route Army when the war broke out, and after 1949 became one of the first directors to make puppet animation. His 1955 The Magic Brush was the first Chinese animation to win awards abroad, bringing back five; the 1963 The Peacock Princess is China's first colour puppet feature.
highlights: China's first colour puppet feature, adapted from the Dai epic poem Zhao Shutun.
Characters designed by painter Cheng Shifa.
Jin Xi's 1955 The Magic Brush was the first Chinese animation to win abroad.
Uses Dai costumes, architecture and dance.
gr26-081.st:
Written by Jin Xi and Yin Kouyang and directed by Jin Xi, the film was produced by the Shanghai Animation Film Studio in 1963 and adapts the Dai epic poem Zhao Shutun, with character designs by painter Cheng Shifa. Puppet animation was the direction Jin explored throughout the early People's Republic: in 1953 he made the first colour puppet film The Little Hero and afterwards reflected that it was influenced by Western Europe and lacked national style; in 1954 he visited Czech puppet master Jiří Trnka at the Karlovy Vary festival and toured his studio, then made The Magic Brush, seen as the beginning of a national style.

The Peacock Princess tells of Prince Zhao Shutun who falls in love with the Peacock Princess, but a treacherous minister's slander forces her to leave and the prince goes through hardships to follow her; running time varies by source (about 73 to 80 minutes). It uses Dai costumes, architecture and dance, an attempt at a feature-length Chinese puppet film.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 流光：动画展映单元
gr26-081.editorial: A puppet film good for children and a record of the craft of Shanghai's animation studio in the 1960s; note the handling of Dai costume and dance.
gr26-081.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Confinement or displacement; Relationship conflict or coercion; Dangerous situations or accidents. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

gr26-082.title: Prince Nezha’s Triumph Against Dragon King
gr26-082.syn: Young Nezha defies the Dragon King to protect his people, sacrificing himself before returning through a miraculous rebirth.
gr26-082.bio: Nezha Conquers the Dragon King was co-directed by Wang Shuchen, Yan Dingxian and Xu Jingda (Ada), with overall art design by painter Zhang Ding, then head of the Central Academy of Arts and Design. Made by the Shanghai Animation Film Studio for the 30th anniversary of the People's Republic in 1979, it is China's first widescreen animated feature.
highlights: China's first widescreen animated feature, made by the Shanghai studio for the 30th anniversary of the PRC.
Painter Zhang Ding as art designer, drawing on Dunhuang and Yongle Palace murals.
Co-directed by three directors over 15 months.
Won the Hundred Flowers award for best art film and showed at Cannes.
gr26-082.st:
A first draft of the script was finished in the late 1950s, when a co-production with the Moscow animation studio was planned; the partnership stopped and the script sat for twenty years. In 1977 the Shanghai studio sought a subject that could carry on national culture while breaking new ground, director Wang Shuchen dug out the script, and it became the key film for the 30th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic, with what was described as the strongest directing team ever. Production began in May 1978 and took 15 months, a hand-drawn tour de force.

Zhang Ding was invited in the summer of 1978 as chief art designer and went from field research to character design in two months; drawing on Dunhuang and Yongle Palace murals and folk New Year prints and woodcuts, he combined decorative lines with the folk palette of cyan, green, red, white and black to achieve an aesthetic that is both familiar and fresh. The story comes from Investiture of the Gods, but the filmmakers did not copy it: Nezha became a lively, endearing youth unafraid of power, and Li Jing a father with tenderness toward his child; Nezha's suicide scene remains vivid for many viewers.

It was released on 19 May 1979, won the Best Art Film prize at the third Hundred Flowers Awards in 1980 and was shown at Cannes; director Jiaozi has said the 1979 version was the starting point of his new Ne Zha.
gr26-082.dir: Wang Shuchen / Yan Dingxian / A Da
gr26-082.editorial: If you have just seen the new Ne Zha, go back to the 1979 source: decorative imagery, Peking-opera rhythm and a youthful hero's tragedy. Nezha's suicide scene is heavy, so take care with young children.
gr26-082.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Harm or death involving children; Self-harm and self-sacrifice; Violence or injury. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.
gr26-082.dirLife: Wang Shuchen · Yan Dingxian · Xu Jingda (Ada) · China

gr26-083.title: Chinese Animation: A Century
gr26-083.syn: Archival footage and artists' recollections trace a century of Chinese animation and the development of its distinctive artistic traditions.
gr26-083.bio: Sun Lijun, former vice president of the Beijing Film Academy and head of the China Animation Research Institute, is chief director of Chinese Animation: A Century, with credits including Little Soldier Zhang Ga and Legend of a Rabbit. Feng Yabing is director and writer, and Yang Zhifeng co-director and editing consultant.
highlights: Reviews a century of Chinese animation, 1922–2022, drawing on more than fifty works.
Interviews over a hundred animators and collects much unreleased material.
Outstanding Film Award at Russia's Northern People International Film Festival in 2024.
Combines live shooting with hand-drawn restoration to reproduce lost techniques.
gr26-083.st:
In December 2022 a seminar titled 'A Century of Chinese Animation: Review, Reflection and Outlook' and the documentary's launch were held; Sun Lijun proposed and led the China Animation Research Institute of the Beijing Film Academy together with the Shanghai Animation Film Studio to launch a series of 'Century of Chinese Animation' activities, of which the film is part. It is a National Publishing Fund project produced by the Ministry of Education's educational technology resource centre with the Shanghai studio.

According to reports, the team prepared for years, consulted millions of words of documents and archives, travelled to more than ten cities and visited the Shanghai Animation Film Studio and other old creative bases, interviewing over a hundred veteran animation artists, industry leaders, scholars and newcomers and collecting many unreleased films, manuscripts, working photos and oral records; it combines traditional live shooting with hand-drawn restoration, reproducing some lost traditional animation techniques. It features more than fifty works including Havoc in Heaven, Where Is Mama, The Legend of Sealed Book, Nezha Conquers the Dragon King, Monkey King: Hero Is Back and Ne Zha.

It opened the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area Animation Film Week in October 2024, was selected in November that year for Russia's Northern People International Film Festival, winning the outstanding film award with a special contribution award for Sun Lijun, and opened in Chinese cinemas on 1 June 2026.
honors: 入选｜2026 Golden Rooster Film Screening · 流光：动画展映单元
gr26-083.editorial: A primer on the Chinese school of animation: see Princess Iron Fan and Nezha Conquers the Dragon King first and it will resonate more. It is a documentary built on archives and interviews.
gr26-083.contentNote: The available synopsis has been reviewed, but no specific sensitive content has been established. This is not an all-ages assurance or a full content assessment.

amrum.title: Amrum
amrum.syn: A historical drama set in spring 1945, in the last days of the Second World War, centred on ten-year-old Nanning. With his father away at the front, the boy does everything he can to help his mother feed the family: hunting seals, fishing at night, working the fields. But the long-awaited peace brings new conflict, and Nanning must find his own course among the ruins.
honors: 提名｜2026 ASC Awards · Spotlight Award
获奖｜2026 Bavarian Film Awards · Best Film
提名｜2026 German Film Awards · Outstanding Feature Film / Best Cinematography / Best Sound / Best Film Score / Best Costume Design / Best Makeup
highlights: The story comes from Hark Bohm's own childhood; Akin took it on as a way of fulfilling a friend's wish, so the film carries both personal memory and a handing-down between directors.
It is Akin's first film about Germany's own wartime history, seen through the eyes of a ten-year-old as the loss of paradise.
Much of the film is about a child finding food for his family: hunting seals, fishing at night, working the fields. Hunger gives the war its most concrete shape.
Shot by Independence Day cinematographer Lindenlaub, the sea, wind and fields of a North Sea island are the stars of the image; the film was nominated for the ASC Spotlight Award.
amrum.bio: Fatih Akin was born in Hamburg in 1973 to a Turkish immigrant family and is one of the most internationally recognised European directors of his generation. He won the Golden Bear in Berlin in 2004 for Head-On (Gegen die Wand), the Special Jury Prize in Venice in 2009 for Soul Kitchen, and competed for the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2017 with In the Fade (Aus dem Nichts), which he co-wrote with Hark Bohm. Amrum is his twelfth feature and the first in which he turns directly to Germany's own wartime history. As a teenager he was deeply influenced by Bohm's films such as Nordsee ist Mordsee and Moritz, lieber Moritz; the two were close friends and mentor and pupil for many years. Bohm died in November 2025 at the age of 86.
amrum.st:
Amrum is drawn from the childhood memories of director Hark Bohm. Bohm had meant to direct it himself; after telling Akin about his childhood, he was encouraged to make it into a film, and in the end he handed the direction to his long-time friend, who rewrote Bohm's original script and directed it. Akin calls the film very special and unusual for him: a journey into the depths of his 'German soul' and, perhaps, the last lesson Bohm taught him.

Shooting ran from 22 April to 25 June 2024 in Hamburg, on the island of Amrum and in Denmark. The cinematographer is Karl Walter Lindenlaub (Independence Day) and the editor Andrew Bird (The Seed of the Sacred Fig, Head-On); it was produced by Akin's Bombero International and Warner Bros. Film Productions Germany with Rialto Film. Twelve-year-old Jasper Billerbeck plays Nanning, Diane Kruger reunites with Akin, and Bohm himself appears as the old man by the sea.

The film had its world premiere on 15 May 2025 in the Cannes Premiere section of the 78th Cannes Film Festival and later won Best Film at the 2026 Bavarian Film Awards. Akin describes the story as an expulsion from paradise: in the last weeks of the war the children are not sent to the front, yet they carry responsibility for their families' food and future.
amrum.editorial: Suited to viewers who like historical drama and coming-of-age stories. Watch the disagreement between the boy and his mother: the end of the war does not mean old ideas at home disappear with it. It also rewards comparison with Akin's earlier work on migration and identity, and how he handles the idea of being German here.
amrum.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Nazi-era persecution and its aftermath; Animal harm or death themes; Family conflict or separation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

dry-leaf.title: Dry Leaf
dry-leaf.syn: Photographer Lisa suddenly disappears. The last clues point to seven football pitches she photographed, scattered across seven remote Georgian villages. Her father Irakli travels from pitch to pitch looking for her, and Lisa's ghost-like best friend Levani quietly joins the search. As the pitches change, villagers and their stories pass by like a carousel. Beneath the seemingly absurd journey, something darker builds: with every pitted field and every silent village, the hope of finding Lisa thins like morning mist.
honors: 提名｜2025 Locarno Film Festival · Golden Leopard, Best Film
获奖｜2025 Locarno Film Festival · Golden Leopard, Special Mention
获奖｜2025 Locarno Film Festival · FIPRESCI Prize
提名｜2025 Entrevues Belfort Film Festival · Grand Prix Janine Bazin
提名｜2025 Hainan Island International Film Festival · Golden Coconut, Best Picture
获奖｜2025 Bangkok International Film Festival · Grand Prix
获奖｜2025 Pančevo International Film Festival · Best Film
highlights: A road movie about searching for a missing daughter that spends most of its time on football pitches, villages and chance encounters.
Shot entirely on an old mobile phone, its rough low-resolution image carries nostalgia and makes people and land hard to tell apart.
Written, shot and edited by the director alone, with music and sound by his brother and his father in the lead: a near-family-workshop way of making a film.
Festival notes call it a whimsical love letter to his homeland, to football, and to art made from nothing.
dry-leaf.bio: Alexandre Koberidze was born in Tbilisi, Georgia, studied directing at the German Film and Television Academy Berlin (DFFB) and lives in Berlin. His early shorts include Der Fall (2014), Colophon (2015) and The Perfect Spectator (2017); his first feature Let the Summer Never Come Again (2017) won the top prize at FIDMarseille, and his second, What Do We See When We Look at the Sky? (2021), premiered at the Berlinale and won the FIPRESCI Prize. Dry Leaf is his third feature: he is writer, cinematographer and editor, his brother Giorgi Koberidze composes the music and designs the sound, and his father David Koberidze plays the lead.
dry-leaf.st:
The title comes from the football term 'folha seca' (Portuguese for 'dry leaf'), a free kick whose landing is hard to predict. Nino and Irakli's daughter Lisa, a sports photographer, vanishes after leaving a letter asking not to be found. Her father cannot let go: he drives across rural Georgia, asking in every town the same question, 'Is there a football field around here?'

The whole film was shot on an old Sony Ericsson W595 mobile phone; the low-resolution image lets people and places merge. In interviews Koberidze talks about the sacrifices of older generations and how the phone sharpened his eye. It is a German-Georgian co-production by New Matter Films and runs 186 minutes.

It had its world premiere on 13 August 2025 in the International Competition of the 78th Locarno Film Festival, winning a Golden Leopard Special Mention and the FIPRESCI Prize, then the Grand Prix at the Bangkok International Film Festival and Best Film at Pančevo, and was named one of the top ten films of 2025 in Sight & Sound's poll.
dry-leaf.editorial: For viewers willing to slow down. Don't rush to ask where the daughter has gone; watch for the football pitch in each town, the small talk and the unforced humour. It runs 186 minutes, so allow plenty of time.
dry-leaf.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Missing loved ones; Emotional distress or trauma. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

i-understand-your-displeasure.title: I Understand Your Displeasure
i-understand-your-displeasure.syn: Heike (59) is a customer service manager at a cleaning company, coordinating between clients, management and the cleaning staff. Her company is in conflict with an important subcontractor because Heike broke the rules trying to poach an informal worker from his team. The subcontractor now threatens to withdraw his support unless she secures more hours and income for him. To satisfy him, Heike has to dismiss one of her own staff, a colleague her friend Taya values highly. Heike feels increasingly torn between her responsibility to her team and the realities of a low-wage industry.
honors: 获奖｜2026 Hong Kong International Film Festival · Young Cinema Competition (World), Best Actress
入围｜2026 Berlin International Film Festival · Panorama
获奖｜2026 First Steps Award · Best Feature Film
获奖｜2026 Kinofest Lünen · Acting Prize for Lead Actress (Sabine Thalau)
highlights: The director has worked in cleaning himself and says he never stops researching, because reality keeps changing; the script is built on that.
Lead actress Sabine Thalau, a non-professional from the cleaning industry, won the Golden Firebird for Best Actress at the Hong Kong International Film Festival.
Instead of accusing, the film follows Heike's series of reasonable-looking decisions and shows how pressure pushes a person into isolation.
A continuation of Nuclear Nomads: more attention to workers rarely seen on screen.
i-understand-your-displeasure.st:
The film takes on the cleaning industry, one of Germany's largest service sectors. The director says it began from personal experience, and from wanting to look at the isolation of a trade in which everyone cleans alone: low pay and a piece-rate rhythm push colleagues to compete instead of standing together. Heike, a team leader, is told that to meet a contract she must sacrifice one of her own employees. As the pressure closes in she revives her dream of founding her own cleaning company, only to find she has burned too many bridges with her colleagues.

The film is shot in a near-observational mode, without sermonising or spectacle. Lead actress Sabine Thalau comes from the cleaning trade and is a non-professional; Friedrich talks about the authenticity she brings. The script is by Friedrich with Tünde Sautier and Daniel Kunz, produced by WennDann Film, with Films Boutique handling world sales.

It premiered on 13 February 2026 in the Panorama section of the 76th Berlinale, then won the First Steps Award for Best Feature Film; Sabine Thalau won the Golden Firebird for Best Actress at the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the lead acting prize at Kinofest Lünen.
i-understand-your-displeasure.editorial: For viewers interested in labour, class and the workplace. Watch each small trade-off Heike makes with her colleagues: individually they make sense, together they reveal the pressure of the system. The pace is tight and the mood oppressive, so you may want some time to decompress afterwards.
i-understand-your-displeasure.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Social inequality or workplace mistreatment; Financial hardship or exploitation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.
i-understand-your-displeasure.bio: Kilian Armando Friedrich was born in Konstanz, Germany, in 1995 and grew up in a border region between France and Germany once shaped by coal and steel; the factories there closed during his childhood. He studied acting in Hildesheim and Madrid, then documentary directing in Munich and Mexico City. Between finishing school and starting university he worked for about eight months in the cleaning industry, the experience this film grew from. His documentary Nuclear Nomads (Nomades du nucléaire), co-directed with Tizian Stromp Zargari and about temporary workers who clean nuclear reactors, premiered at the Berlinale in 2023 and won the German Short Film Award in the medium-length category. I Understand Your Displeasure is his first fiction feature.

karla.title: Karla
karla.syn: Set in Munich in 1962, the film tells the true story of 12-year-old Karla, who files a complaint against her father, seeking protection from his years of abuse. As she navigates the legal system, she forms a special bond with Judge Lamy, who becomes her beacon of hope. Karla is reluctant to reveal the full extent of her suffering, which gradually forces Judge Lamy to give her the freedom to tell her story on her own terms, a choice that puts his own career at risk.
honors: 获奖｜2026 Bavarian Film Awards · Best Screenplay, Best Actor
获奖｜2025 Munich Film Festival · German Cinema New Talent Award, Best Director and Best Screenplay
提名｜2026 Göteborg Film Festival · Ingmar Bergman Award, Best Debut Feature
highlights: Based on a real 1962 case: a twelve-year-old walks into a police station and takes her father to court.
The film uses flashbacks with restraint and shows no violence, saving its strength for how a child comes to be heard.
Lead actress Elise Krieps appears in a film for the first time; the Luxembourg film festival called it an impressive breakout role.
Directed and written by women, it won the German Cinema New Talent Awards for Best Director and Best Screenplay at the Munich Film Festival.
karla.bio: Christina Tournatzés (also spelled Tournatzès) was born in 1992 to a German-Greek background, lives in Munich, and graduated in 2019 from Macromedia University of Applied Sciences in Munich, where she studied directing. Karla is her first feature, written by Yvonne Görlach and produced by achtung panda! in Munich, with international sales handled by The Playmaker Munich; it was shown to international buyers at the 2025 Cannes film market. The film reflects her interest in trauma wrapped in silence and in the position of children within institutions.
karla.st:
The film is based on a real 1962 case in Munich: after studying law in the library, twelve-year-old Karla walks into a police station and asks to see a judge, to bring charges against the father who has abused her for years. One review calls it a milestone German case, the first in which a child sought a legal response to an abusive parent. Through discreet flashbacks, director Christina Tournatzés and cinematographer Florian Emmerich only hint at what happened, keeping the focus on how she finds the words and who is willing to listen.

Judge Lamy (Rainer Bock) takes the case on reluctantly; Karla's refusal to disclose everything at once forces him to give her the freedom to tell her story on her own terms, at risk to his own career. The trust that gradually forms between them is the film's emotional axis. Lead actress Elise Krieps, daughter of Vicky Krieps, makes her screen debut; German actors such as Imogen Kogge (The Zone of Interest) and Rainer Bock (The White Ribbon) support her.

It premiered at the Munich Film Festival in June 2025, winning German Cinema New Talent Awards for Best Director and Best Screenplay, was nominated in the Ingmar Bergman Competition for debuts at the Gothenburg Film Festival, and won Best Screenplay and Best Lead Performance at the 2026 Bavarian Film Awards.
karla.editorial: For viewers concerned with children's rights, the law and social silence. Watch how the judge and Karla slowly build trust, and how the film shows what it means to be believed. The subject is child abuse; it is told with restraint but is emotionally heavy, so please choose according to your own circumstances.
warnings: Violence against women or domestic abuse
karla.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Child abuse; Violence against women or domestic abuse; Distressing legal proceedings. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

miroirs-no-3.title: Miroirs No. 3
miroirs-no-3.syn: On a weekend trip to the countryside, Laura miraculously survives a car crash. Physically unharmed but deeply shaken, she is taken in by Betty, a witness to the accident, who cares for her attentively. Gradually Betty's husband and son also accept Laura's presence, and a family-like calm returns to the house. But before long, the shadows of the past come back…
honors: 提名｜2025 Cannes Film Festival · Directors’ Fortnight
提名｜2025 Sydney Film Festival · Sydney Film Prize, Best Film
highlights: The title comes from Ravel's 'A Boat on the Ocean'; the music echoes a story of a drifting person taken in.
Petzold's fourth consecutive collaboration with Paula Beer, whose relationship is the core of his recent films.
He calls it a ghost story and another variation on Vertigo; mirrors and doubles recur as themes.
At only 86 minutes; Reverse Shot's review calls it a softer film than Petzold has ever made.
miroirs-no-3.bio: Christian Petzold was born in Hilden, Germany, in 1960 and is a leading figure of the Berlin School. He won the Silver Bear for Best Director in Berlin in 2012 for Barbara; his later films Phoenix (2014), Transit, Undine (2020) and Afire (2023) were all acclaimed internationally, and Afire won the Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. He has long worked with actress Paula Beer; Miroirs No. 3 is their fourth consecutive collaboration, his eleventh feature, and his first selection at Cannes. He is also the new president of the Viennale, which opened its 2025 edition with this film.
miroirs-no-3.st:
The title comes from the third piece of Ravel's piano suite Miroirs, 'Une barque sur l'océan' (A Boat on the Ocean). Petzold says the idea first came to him while shooting Afire. Laura (Paula Beer), a piano student, survives a serious car accident and is taken in by a grieving family; between her and the lady of the house, Betty (Barbara Auer), a mirror-like resonance slowly develops. In his Directors' Fortnight interview Petzold admits it is a ghost story and another variation on Hitchcock's Vertigo.

Shooting began in August 2024 with long-time collaborator Hans Fromm behind the camera. The film had its world premiere on 17 May 2025 in the Directors' Fortnight at the 78th Cannes Film Festival and then played the New York Film Festival and the Viennale. Reverse Shot's review calls it Petzold's softest film to date: its slipperiness comes not from the unknown, as in Phoenix or Transit, but from the unacknowledged.
miroirs-no-3.editorial: For fans of Petzold, European art cinema and psychological suspense. Watch the mirroring between characters: who stands in for whom, who is seen by whom. The pace is restrained and little is explained, so viewers fill in the gaps themselves.
miroirs-no-3.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Dangerous situations or accidents; Psychological distress or uncertainty; Family conflict or separation. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.

the-miserable-mother.title: The Miserable Mother
the-miserable-mother.syn: A young mother trapped by housework, a Peter Pan-like boyfriend who never grows up, and a newborn baby. Fairies descend, the baby speaks, an angel appears: surreal, fantastical elements arrive one after another in song and dance. The film blends the aesthetic language of classic musicals, with the dreamy palette of Jacques Demy's The Umbrellas of Cherbourg and the bold borrowing of soap-opera structure from Chantal Akerman's Golden Eighties. Director Susanne Heinrich weaves in the language of contemporary social media for a dazzling modern musical spectacle. Beneath the singing and dancing lies a mother's inner journey to find her own boundaries.
honors: 获奖｜2026 Munich Film Festival · German Cinema New Talent Award, Best Screenplay
获奖｜2026 Shanghai International Film Festival · Golden Goblet, Outstanding Artistic Achievement
获奖｜2026 Palić Film Festival · International Competition, Special Mention
highlights: A musical about new motherhood that turns childcare, the division of labour at home and society's expectations of the 'good mother' into things that can be sung and danced.
The second part of the trilogy on female subjectivity, continuing the questions about women under late capitalism raised in Aren't You Happy?
The director also writes the lyrics; the music was made with Willi Sieger and others, and the songs and physical performance carry much of the narrative.
It won the Outstanding Artistic Achievement award at the Shanghai International Film Festival and Best Screenplay at Munich's German Cinema New Talent Awards.
the-miserable-mother.bio: Susanne Heinrich was born in Leipzig in 1985 and is director, writer and one of the film's songwriters. Her first feature, Das melancholische Mädchen (Aren't You Happy?, 2019), premiered at the Max Ophüls Prize festival and won Best Film. The Miserable Mother is the second part of her trilogy on female subjectivity, which looks at the condition of womanhood in late capitalism; the third part, The Outdated Woman, is in development.
the-miserable-mother.st:
The film is a musical: a woman who has just given birth is shut in by her own four walls, and the boundaries between inside and outside, society and individual, body and discourse begin to blur. Her partner 'Peter Pan' (Theo Colarusso) does his best to 'help' but keeps dodging her anger, literally dancing around it. Newcomer Rosa Landers plays the Mother in her biggest role to date.

It was shot in Leipzig from 11 June to 17 July 2024, with cinematography by Agnesh Pakozdi and music by Willi Sieger, produced by reynard films (Leipzig) with Coproduction Office, and runs 81 minutes. Screen Daily calls it a wry, sincere study of new motherhood, with a keen sense of fury, awe and mischief.

In 2026 it won Best Screenplay in the German Cinema New Talent strand at the Munich Film Festival and the Outstanding Artistic Achievement award in the Golden Goblet competition at the Shanghai International Film Festival, as well as a Special Mention in the International Competition at the Palić European Film Festival.
the-miserable-mother.editorial: For viewers who like formal experiment, feminism and musicals. Treat the songs as dialogue: they are both self-mockery and a rebuttal of how a mother 'should' be. The style is exaggerated, funny and sharp, and does not aim at realism.

oh-this-unspeakable-void.title: Oh This Unspeakable Void
oh-this-unspeakable-void.syn: At twenty, Joachim is unexpectedly accepted into the renowned acting school in Munich and moves into the villa of his grandparents, Inge and Hermann. Between the bizarre challenges of drama school and his grandparents' eccentric, mostly alcohol-fuelled rituals, Joachim tries to find his place in the world, without knowing what role he actually plays in it.
honors: 获奖｜2026 German Film Awards · Best Film, 2nd Runner-up (Bronze)
获奖｜2026 German Film Awards · Best Actress (Senta Berger)
获奖｜2026 German Film Awards · Best Supporting Actor (Michael Wittenborn)
highlights: Adapted from Meyerhoff's autobiographical bestseller, it blends the oddities of drama-school life with warmth between grandparents and grandson.
Mother and son on one project: director Simon Verhoeven cast his own mother, Senta Berger, as the grandmother, and at 85 she won her first German Film Award for Best Actress.
A strong ensemble including Karoline Herfurth, Tom Schilling, Laura Tonke and Friedrich von Thun.
The Süddeutsche Zeitung called it a light-handed heavy literary adaptation; Filmstarts called it the funniest German film in years.
oh-this-unspeakable-void.bio: Simon Verhoeven was born in Munich in 1972, the son of actress Senta Berger and director Michael Verhoeven (who died in April 2024). He established himself with the comedies Männerherzen and Willkommen bei den Hartmanns (2016), the latter one of Germany's biggest recent box-office hits, followed by Alter weißer Mann (2022) and Girl You Know It's True (2023), about Milli Vanilli. Oh, This Unspeakable Void is adapted from Joachim Meyerhoff's autobiographical bestseller, co-written with Lars Hubrich; the grandmother is played by his own mother, Senta Berger.
oh-this-unspeakable-void.st:
The film is adapted from Joachim Meyerhoff's 2015 novel of the same name, the third volume of his cycle Alle Toten fliegen hoch. Twenty-year-old Joachim (Bruno Alexander) is unexpectedly accepted at Munich's renowned Otto Falckenberg School of the Performing Arts and moves into his grandparents' villa in Munich, facing the odd methods of acting training while living with a grandmother (Senta Berger) and grandfather of strong character. The cycle's second volume has already been filmed.

It was shot in Munich, Cologne and Berlin, runs 137 minutes and opened in Germany on 29 January 2026, with Karoline Herfurth, Tom Schilling, Laura Tonke and others in the cast. The Süddeutsche Zeitung called it a light-handed heavy literary adaptation, and Filmstarts called it the funniest German film in years.

It received seven nominations at the 2026 German Film Awards and won three: Outstanding Feature Film (Bronze), Best Actress for Senta Berger, who won her first German Film Award at 85, and Best Supporting Actor for Michael Wittenborn.
oh-this-unspeakable-void.editorial: For viewers who like literary adaptations, coming-of-age comedies and stories about acting. Watch the grandmother: she is the funniest and heaviest part of the film, and behind the jokes is a repeated return to the gap of the title. It runs 137 minutes at a relaxed pace.

sometimes-i-imagine-them-all-at-a-party.title: Sometimes, I Imagine Them All at a Party
sometimes-i-imagine-them-all-at-a-party.syn: Fourteen years ago, filmmaker Daniela Magnani Hüller survived an attempted femicide. Now she revisits the key moments of that period of her life. Travelling back and forth between Munich and Rio de Janeiro, she seeks out some of the people who were around her at the time and asks the questions that have haunted her for years. Carefully composed images sketch a complex picture of everything she went through.
honors: 获奖｜2026 Berlin International Film Festival · Forum, Berlinale Documentary Award Jury Special Mention
获奖｜2026 DOK.fest München · Student Award
highlights: The director draws on her own experience, refuses pity and asks who bears responsibility, placing a seemingly private event back within the justice system and society.
The film has both a factual strand and a felt one: conversations with police, doctor and teacher, and tactile imagery of dolls and butterflies.
In the Brazil chapters she reunites with her half-sister, and the shift in colour and rhythm lets the film breathe.
It won a Special Mention for the Berlinale Documentary Award, and Cineuropa called it a formally complex, sensitive and unflinchingly direct autobiographical film.
sometimes-i-imagine-them-all-at-a-party.st:
The film is an autobiographical documentary: in her last year of high school, years ago, the director was subjected to harassment, stalking and threats by a classmate and finally survived a knife attack. Years later she returns to the people involved at the time, including a policewoman, a doctor, a teacher, a schoolmate and the school's legal expert who accompanied her to court, to ask them questions again, and examines how the justice system works and where it fails to protect victims of violence. The factual strand is shot in high-resolution digital with tactile imagery woven in; when she travels to Brazil to reunite with her half-sister, grey Munich gives way to vibrant Rio and lush nature, implying a rebirth, or at least an attempt at one.

In her director's statement she says she believes one can go on living without bitterness after violence, but with an appropriate and perhaps necessary anger. The film is produced by Bildersturm Filmproduktion with ZDF Das kleine Fernsehspiel; producer Birgit Schulz, cinematographer Noah Böhm, editor Melanie Jilg.

It had its world premiere on 15 February 2026 in the Forum of the 76th Berlinale, where it shared a Special Mention for the Berlinale Documentary Award; in May it won the megaherz Student Award at DOK.fest München and opened in German cinemas on 14 May.
sometimes-i-imagine-them-all-at-a-party.editorial: The film's subject is a real act of violence, lived by the director and told in the film; it is emotionally heavy, so please consider your own circumstances before watching. For viewers concerned with gender-based violence, the justice system and self-narration. The pace is calm; watch how tenderness and anger coexist in the images.
warnings: Violence against women or domestic abuse

sometimes-i-imagine-them-all-at-a-party.bio: Daniela Magnani Hüller was born in Munich in 1995 and is a German-Brazilian filmmaker. After a bachelor's degree in media and communication she began studying documentary directing at the University of Television and Film Munich (HFF) in 2019, making several self-written, self-directed and self-edited shorts including Frei sein (2020), Atide and Driving Force (2022), Arthrocalypse (2023) and Rauswachsen (2024), and won the DOK.talent Award at DOK.fest München in 2023. Sometimes, I Imagine Them All at a Party is her autobiographical documentary feature debut, in which she returns to an attempted femicide she survived at 17.

when-pigs-fly.title: When Pigs Fly
when-pigs-fly.syn: Is my heart a part of me? Does it share my experiences? Or is it merely a lump of flesh, a muscle, a pump, an organ easily replaced by another? In our society, pigs are only considered valuable once they are dead, even though they are so similar to humans that their hearts can be used as donor organs. In a future in which hearts are grown in pigs to save human lives, the line between the two species begins to blur. Is this the moment to rethink the human–pig relationship? The film follows two veterinarians in their ambivalent relationship with pigs, and offers intimate access to an animal that is far closer to us than most people are willing to admit.
honors: 获奖｜2026 DOK.fest München · Audience Award
入围｜2026 DOK.fest München · Competition
入围｜2026 CPH:DOX
highlights: It starts from the seemingly simple question of what a pig is, and opens onto agriculture, pets, ethics and xenotransplantation.
Michael Kalb produced and the director also helped edit; it runs only 80 minutes.
Felix Riedelsheimer is the cinematographer, with sound by Philip Hutter.
It won the audience award at DOK.fest München, decided by audience votes.
when-pigs-fly.st:
Is a pig a farm animal, or something to cuddle? And if pig hearts can soon be transplanted into humans, what entirely new questions will that raise? The film starts from these questions; its working title was Ein Herz (A Heart), and it explores the most intimate and contradictory relationships between pigs and humans. The cinematographer is Felix Riedelsheimer, the editors are Melanie Jilg, Hauke von Stietencron and the director, the music is by Marja Burchard, and it is produced by Michael Kalb Filmproduktion. It runs 80 minutes in English and German.

It had its world premiere at CPH:DOX in Copenhagen on 14 March 2026 and its German premiere at DOK.fest München on 9 May, then won the kinokino Audience Award, sponsored by BR and 3sat. The award, worth 2,000 euros, is decided by audience members voting by QR code after each screening; the film led the audience ranking at one point during the festival.
when-pigs-fly.editorial: For viewers concerned with animal ethics, food and medicine. The film discusses pig farming and medical use and may include animal-related imagery whose intensity has not been verified; it is brisk at 80 minutes and suits viewers who come with questions.
when-pigs-fly.contentNote: Available story information indicates: Animal harm or death themes; Illness, treatment or care. Detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified; consider your individual needs.
when-pigs-fly.bio: Denise Riedmayr studied documentary directing at the University of Television and Film Munich (HFF) and works as a freelance filmmaker and as author, director and editor for Bayerischer Rundfunk. She received the City of Munich's Starter Film Award in 2021; her shorts include An Anna (2020) and, co-directed, Swim for Good (2018). When Pigs Fly continues her interest in lived experience and the relationship between humans and animals.

shame-and-money.title: Shame and Money
shame-and-money.syn: After losing their livelihood in the village, a Kosovar family is forced to move to the capital to find a place in a hyper-capitalist society. Shame and Money portrays hard-working people striving for a decent life under relentless pressure and long-term turmoil. Shaban, a traditional head of the household, longs to be the family's pillar, yet it is his mother's savings that keep them afloat. Accepting help from a wealthy brother-in-law brings new challenges. As his pride erodes and his dignity slips away, Shaban edges toward breaking point: how much more can he take?
honors: 获奖｜2026 Munich Film Festival · ARRI/OSRAM Award, Best International Film
获奖｜2026 Sundance Film Festival · World Cinema Dramatic, Grand Jury Prize
提名｜2026 Sydney Film Festival · Sydney Film Prize, Best Film
highlights: Sundance 2026 World Cinema Dramatic Grand Jury Prize; the jury praised the director's deep empathy for his characters at a crucial moment when they are beginning again.
RogerEbert.com called it austere yet hard-hitting, revealing the apathy of a system without melodramatic speeches.
A co-production of six countries, Germany, Kosovo, Slovenia, Albania, North Macedonia and Belgium: a typical Balkan co-produced drama.
Written with Doruntina Basha, it continues Morina's attention to Kosovar society and migration from Babai and Exile.
shame-and-money.bio: Visar Morina was born in Pristina, Kosovo, in 1979 when it was still part of Yugoslavia, and has lived and worked in Germany since 1993. His debut feature Babai (Father) won Best Director at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in 2015; his second, Exile (2020), was nominated for the World Cinema Dramatic Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, its script having won the German Screenplay Award in 2018. Shame and Money is his third feature and his second in Sundance's World Cinema competition, where this time he won the Grand Jury Prize. He co-wrote with Doruntina Basha and is also one of the producers.
shame-and-money.st:
The film follows Shaban (Astrit Kabashi) and Hatixhe (Flonja Kodheli), a middle-aged couple from the Kosovar countryside. After a man named Liridon steals their money and disappears, the family loses its livelihood and must move to the capital, Pristina, to find a place in a hyper-commodified city. With a restrained camera and unsentimental dialogue, Morina peels back, layer by layer, how a decent person loses dignity step by step under globalisation and late capitalism, so that the two words of the title, shame and money, pull against each other.

It is produced by Schuldenberg Films as a co-production of Germany, Kosovo, Slovenia, Albania, North Macedonia and Belgium, shot by Janis Mazuch, and runs 129 minutes.

It had its world premiere on 25 January 2026 in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at Sundance, where Cineuropa called it an early critical standout of the section, and won the Grand Jury Prize. The jury praised his deep empathy for his characters at a crucial moment when they are beginning again. It later won the ARRI/OSRAM Award for Best International Film at the Munich Film Festival.
shame-and-money.editorial: For viewers concerned with migration, class and globalisation. Watch how the couple talk at each moment of forced compromise and how money gradually changes their sense of shame. It runs 129 minutes at a steady pace with a subdued mood.

gh63-054.syn: The Puig family has seven children, and today is the wedding of the youngest, Jacques. It is March 1978 in the suburbs of Nantes. The father is not attending the wedding, as he has been banished from the family. The brothers and sisters, however, are all there, happy to be reunited. Jacques is marrying Martine, a love match for them both. But can love heal the wounds of childhood?
gh63-054.editorial: One wedding banquet slowly opens three generations' old wounds. Watch the choreography and dialogue rhythm of a large ensemble, and the family power beneath the festivity.

gh63-054.bio: Christophe Honoré works in literature and cinema. His films include Love Songs, Sorry Angel and Winter Boy.

gh63-055.syn: Lucy, a concert pianist, has relocated her family from the city to a country house, hoping to ease her husband Philip's severe burnout. Isolated and desperate to protect her young son, Lucy must face the situation alone, trapped between the man she loves and the fear of what he may have done.

gh63-057.title: Diary of a Mad Old Man
gh63-057.syn: Recovering from a stroke, 69-year-old widower Utsugi is confined to his home and dependent on his daughter-in-law Susu for care. As his desire for her intensifies, he begins interpreting her kindness as sexual invitation. Their increasingly charged encounters blur the boundaries between seduction and delusion, intimacy and manipulation, revealing a profound longing for human connection beneath Utsugi's obsession.

gh63-058.title: Possible Love
gh63-058.syn: Mi-ok lives quietly with her unemployed husband Ho-seok and their young son until a funeral brings them into the orbit of affluent couple Ye-ji and Sang-woo. When Ye-ji, a documentary filmmaker chronicling laid-off workers, begins filming Mi-ok, the two women grow close. Meanwhile, Mi-ok finds herself drawn to Sang-woo, as hidden desires and contrasting circumstances begin to unsettle both marriages.
gh63-058.editorial: Class difference enters two marriages and the ethics of filming others. For viewers willing to follow dense relationships step by step and think about where kindness crosses a line.

gh63-058.bio: Born in Daegu in 1954, Lee Chang-dong wrote fiction and taught before directing films, and also served as South Korea’s culture minister. His work includes Peppermint Candy, Oasis, Secret Sunshine, Poetry and Burning. Possible Love reunites him with Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu.
gh63-058.st: Lee Chang-dong’s first feature in eight years grew from his response to a mass layoff and the violent suppression of a strike in South Korea. In his Venice notes he questions what it means to turn workers’ lives into fiction. His script with Oh Jung-mi puts a similar question to Yeji and Miok. Kim Ji-yong shot the film, Jung Jaeil composed the score, and Netflix began streaming it on November 6, 2026.
highlights: Follow who asks questions and who has the freedom to refuse an answer, at the funeral and in the documentary.
On the shared holiday, watch who can afford to relax and who has to think about the next pay cheque.

gh63-060.syn: Garance is a gifted young actress whose talent has yet to bring her the recognition she craves. Living paycheck to paycheck in Paris while struggling with anxiety and alcohol addiction, she finds solace in caring for her sick younger sister and a blossoming romance with Pauline. As these relationships deepen, Garance begins a difficult but transformative journey towards confronting her past and rebuilding her life.

gh63-061.title: The Beloved
gh63-061.syn: The acclaimed film director Esteban Martínez is a legend both for his films and for his past marked by violence and excess. For his new project, he offers his daughter Emilia a role under the pretext of helping her with her stalled acting career. Living together on set will foster a closeness they haven't shared for years, but it will also reopen old wounds that never healed.
gh63-061.editorial: A father–daughter bond and set hierarchy reflect each other. Aspect ratio, black-and-white and the shoot itself make the filmmaker one of those being examined.

gh63-062.syn: Sixteen-year-old Pyteh splits his time between the wrestling mat and his family's struggling Circassian diner in Newark. A single impulsive decision by his hustling father changes the course of his life, shaping a tale of pride, legacy, and masculinity.
gh63-062.editorial: The frustrations of fathers and sons in an immigrant family surface through sports training. For those interested in physical performance, male expectations and belonging.

gh63-063.title: Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty!
gh63-063.syn: Middle-aged Haru and her husband Luis are serious about ballroom dancing, performing the rumba, tango, and paso doble in competitions across Tokyo. But after enduring a catastrophic loss, Haru loses her spark. Nine months on, her sister and cousin cajole her back into the studio, where a sexy new dance instructor, Fedir, might just pull her out of her rut and ignite an unexpected attraction.

gh63-065.title: Death Has No Master

When legal action proves ineffectual, Caro decides to dispense justice herself, unearthing histories of violence in the process.

gh63-066.title: Falling House
gh63-066.syn: A modest family on the outskirts of Tehran faces the imminent destruction of their home as part of a vast redevelopment project. As the bulldozers draw ever closer, the tensions within the household start to rise.

gh63-067.title: NAZA
gh63-067.syn: Filmed at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, this documentary investigates the systems and decision- making behind Israeli military strikes in Gaza. Through secret conversations with 24 military and intelligence insiders, two Israeli filmmakers examine targeting practices, surveillance technology, and calculations of anticipated civilian casualties, while questioning the mechanisms that enable the dehumanisation and mass killing of Palestinian civilians.
gh63-067.editorial: Anonymous testimony and intelligence technology make responsibility for war concrete. For fans of investigative documentary; accounts of civilian casualties call for some emotional preparation.

gh63-068.title: Rehearsals for a Revolution
gh63-068.syn: Through five portraits of relatives and mentors, five expressions of resistance, Pegah Ahangarani sketches her life story. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, protest footage, newspapers, and recorded voices, she retraces 40 years of Iran's history. From the early days of 1979 until the war that began in 2026, she pieces together intimate and collective memories, forming the portrait of a country shaped by political repression and in constant hope for revolution.
gh63-068.editorial: Private archives re-thread forty years of political change. Across five chapters, family experience and revolutionary memory speak to each other on different levels.

gh63-069.title: Yo (Love Is a Rebellious Bird)
gh63-069.syn: After the death of her beloved friend Yo, filmmaker Anna Fitch spends a decade building a one-third- scale replica of Yo's house, where memories and imagination intertwine. Blending intimate footage from Yo's final year with creative reimaginings of her remarkable life, the film celebrates a friendship that transcends age and death while exploring the power of artistic creation to transform grief into love.
gh63-069.editorial: Making miniature houses and puppets is a way of remembering a friend. For those who like handmade materials, intimate documentary and gentle imagination.
gh63-069.contentNote: Story information indicates: Death and grief. Compiled from the synopsis and public information; detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified, so please consider your individual needs.

gh63-070.title: Silenced
gh63-070.syn: After #MeToo shattered the silence surrounding gendered violence, survivors found themselves facing a new threat as defamation laws were weaponised against those who spoke out. International human rights lawyer Jennifer Robinson follows high-profile legal battles across the world, exposing how the justice system is used to silence, discredit, and financially ruin survivors and the journalists reporting their stories.
gh63-070.editorial: Puts defamation law back into the reality of survivors speaking out. For those interested in public issues and legal mechanisms: the focus is who gets to speak and at what cost.
gh63-070.contentNote: Story information indicates: Sexual violence and harassment. Compiled from the synopsis and public information; detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified, so please consider your individual needs.

gh63-071.title: Wishful Thinking
gh63-071.syn: Julia, an ambitious game designer, and Charlie, a struggling musician, are striving to repair their volatile relationship. After attending a couples-therapy seminar run by mysterious twin healers, they discover that the state of their relationship has supernatural effects on the world around them. With earthquakes, the stock market, and entire nations at risk, Julia and Charlie must decide whether their passionate love can survive the resulting chaos.
gh63-071.editorial: A couple's emotions can change the world, turning lovers' quarrels into fantasy comedy. Split screens and long takes make the ups and downs of a relationship visible.

gh63-073.title: The End of It
gh63-073.syn: In a future where ageing has been cured and death is optional, Claire decides to end her life as she approaches her 250th birthday. Her choice unsettles her husband, daughter, and AI assistant, exposing the complexities of their relationships. As Claire embraces death as her final artistic act, she is forced to confront what it truly means to live, die, and create.
gh63-073.editorial: Living forever doesn't necessarily mean having a future. For fans of sci-fi black comedy: an exaggerated premise to think about ageing, creativity and autonomy.

gh63-074.title: Dua
gh63-074.syn: Prishtina, Kosovo, late 1990s. As war looms and ethnic tensions escalate, 13-year-old Dua struggles to find her place among her peers and within her changing body. After an incident shakes her community, she becomes a target herself and bonds with a fearless girl, Maki, who draws her toward an unexpected form of resistance. Between the violence and the growing threat of exile, there is little room for quiet awakenings.
gh63-074.editorial: War closes in from the background, yet a girl's daily life still carries resistance. Notice the violence never shown directly, and the strength in her friendships.

gh63-075.title: The Guest

As they confront the lingering wounds of their past, Audrey and Eli discover the possibility of healing through love, despite the weight of family, guilt, and loss.

Their lives shift when Colin, a teenager raised on the American base, enters their circle. gh63-089.title: Our Share of Sand
gh63-089.syn: After years apart, 12-year-old Maya returns to India with her mother to reunite with her father, who runs a sand-mining business. She befriends Kiran, a young worker, but when an accident leaves him permanently injured, Maya becomes a key witness. With her father relying on her account to clear his name, she begins searching for the truth, uncovering exploitation, deception, and her family's complicity.

gh63-089.bio: Chilean-born Shalini Adnani has Indian roots and trained in London. White Ant preceded her feature debut Our Share of Sand.

gh63-090.title: The World Before
gh63-090.syn: Seventeen-year-old Jin has never left the remote island where she was born. When her childhood friend Dujae returns for his grandmother's funeral, she begins finding excuses to visit him, and their reunion gradually becomes part of her everyday life. As summer passes, the familiar roads, sea, and faces around her begin to feel different, prompting Jin to see both her island home and herself anew.

gh63-091.title: Nagi Notes
gh63-091.syn: Yoriko, an artist living in rural Nagi, is haunted by a former love affair she cannot bear to mourn. When Yuri, a recently separated architect, travels from Tokyo to visit her friend and former sister-in-law, both women find themselves at a crossroads, searching for ways to let go of the past and define their identities. Yuri's brief escape becomes a quiet confrontation of loss and probing.

gh63-092.title: Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?
gh63-092.syn: Born into poverty in New York, Allen Nelson joins the Marine Corps at 18 and is sent to Vietnam, where the brutal realities of combat shatter his dreams of military glory. Returning home at 23, he is haunted by memories of the battlefield and struggles to reconnect with his family. As his life unravels, a psychiatrist at a veterans' hospital offers him a lifeline.
gh63-092.editorial: A veteran's memories carry war into postwar life. For followers of anti-war cinema; its violence and accounts of trauma call for preparation.

gh63-093.title: Children Untold
gh63-093.syn: In the ruins of post-war Tokyo, 12-year-old Kotoko loses her home and family and is left to survive alone. Realising that being a girl puts her in danger, she conceals her identity and lives as a boy, joining a group of orphaned children. As they struggle through the chaos and hardship of a shattered city, Kotoko discovers companionship, resilience, and the people willing to believe in their future.

gh63-094.title: Between Two Lovers
gh63-094.syn: Children's book author Uta has been married to Morio for three years, while continuing a relationship with her editor and lover, Junna. Unable to choose between them, nor to embrace the idea of having a child with Morio, Uta proposes an unconventional solution: the three of them should live together. Initially met with anger, her proposal takes an unexpected turn after an incident reshapes their relationship.

gh63-095.title: Fujiko
gh63-095.syn: Determined, combative, and indomitable, Fujiko is the kind of woman who scares men, especially in 1970s Japan. After enduring a tyrannical mother-in-law and a stormy divorce, she chooses to raise her daughter Mari as a single mother. Taking on a series of low-paying jobs before becoming an insurance saleswoman, Fujiko faces life's obstacles with humour, resilience, and grit, refusing to surrender to societal pressures.

gh63-096.title: In My Father's Room
gh63-096.syn: Satomi works at an art museum until a mysterious key arrives in an envelope, leading her to a hidden room that once belonged to her father, who died alone a month earlier. Retracing his final days, she discovers a man seemingly left behind by society yet sustained by his devotion to words, the art of tea, and subtle beauty, gradually uncovering the quiet grace of his solitary world.
gh63-096.editorial: A dead man's belongings let his daughter get to know her silent father anew. For fans of art, everyday objects and restrained family stories; don't rush to a dramatic answer.
gh63-096.contentNote: Story information indicates: Family conflict. Compiled from the synopsis and public information; detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified, so please consider your individual needs.
gh63-096.bio: Maha Harada is a novelist and curator with experience at MoMA. In My Father's Room adapts her own writing for her directing debut.

gh63-097.title: To Be Ordinary
gh63-097.syn: After an accident leaves a young man paralysed, his family struggles to rebuild their lives. His mother holds on to hope, his unemployed father becomes his caregiver, and he finds love with his physical therapist. The accident ironically brings the family closer, but his little sister hasn't forgotten that this pretty new home is built on her brother's tragedy. With fate proving unpredictable, deeper tests await both families.

gh63-098.title: Shadow Work
gh63-098.syn: Fleeing her abusive husband, Noriko takes refuge at Ouchi, a secluded shelter where women share responsibilities and rebuild their lives together. But beneath its peaceful façade, Ouchi harbors a secret that binds its residents. Meanwhile, detective Kaoru, herself trapped in an abusive marriage, investigates a series of mysterious crimes that leads her towards Ouchi and its dangerous hidden truth.

gh63-099.title: The Seoul Guardians
gh63-099.syn: On December 3, 2024, South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol declares martial law, banning political activity and public assemblies as troops advance on the National Assembly. Lawmakers race to enter the building and overturn the decree, while citizens gather outside to block the soldiers. As elite troops launch an assault, memories of the Gwangju Uprising resonate through the unfolding confrontation.

gh63-099.bio: Kim Jong-woo, Kim Shin-wan and Cho Cheol-young bring MBC television, journalism and public-affairs experience to their first documentary feature.

gh63-100.title: Prosecution
gh63-100.syn: Far-right violence in eastern Germany is more than what it seems; young prosecutor Seyo Kim learned it the hard way. After surviving a racist attack herself, she defies orders from her superiors and launches her own investigation. As she reopens long-closed cases and uncovers links to a wider extremist network, Seyo is forced to confront a justice system that downplays – and at times protects – the very violence it claims to prosecute.

gh63-101.syn: Seventeen-year-old Sara is hiding a secret during a school trip. When the trip spirals out of control and she witnesses her friend Lina being assaulted, the two girls try to break the cycle of casual violence, sealing an everlasting bond between them.

gh63-102.title: A Place to Heal
gh63-102.syn: Seventeen-year-old Lucia is brought by police to a psychiatric ward she knows all too well. There, she reunites with her friend Eloïse and meets other teenagers confronting their own struggles. As overstretched doctors and caregivers support the young patients and their families, fragile bonds offer moments of hope and laughter. But the arrival of a mysterious new patient, Enzo, threatens to disrupt their delicate balance.

gh63-102.editorial: The people in the psychiatric ward are, first of all, teenagers growing up. Its realist ensemble holds friendship, desire and trauma without reducing anyone to a diagnosis.

highlights: The title 15/18 refers to the adolescent psychiatric ward of a French public hospital, which only admits patients aged 15 to 18. Cédric Kahn again works with a near-documentary structure, stressing how much people on the margins depend on social institutions while facing the pressure those institutions put on individuals. It avoids easy moral verdicts and keeps looking for answers to problems that are not binary, even if the search ends in sadness: a humane return of Italian neorealism today.

gh63-103.title: Sunny Dancer
gh63-103.syn: After 17-year-old Ivy beats cancer, she can think of nothing worse than becoming a Make-A-Wish kid. Sent by her overbearing parents to a summer camp for young people affected by cancer, she struggles to fit in. But as the weeks pass, Ivy finds unexpected friendship among a group of like-minded misfits determined to live life to the fullest.
gh63-103.editorial: Youth at a summer camp for patients doesn't have to be inspirational all the time. For fans of rebellious coming-of-age comedy: see how humour makes room for fear and fragility.
gh63-103.contentNote: Story information indicates: Death and grief. Compiled from the synopsis and public information; detailed depiction and intensity have not been verified, so please consider your individual needs.
gh63-103.bio: British filmmaker and actor George Jaques made his feature debut with Black Dog before Sunny Dancer, continuing his attention to young characters.

gh63-104.title: Sad Girlz
gh63-104.syn: Sixteen-year-old Paula and her best friend La Maestra are the strongest swimmers on their team, training to represent Mexico at the Junior Pan American Swimming Championship. But after a party leaves Paula traumatised, the two girls struggle to make sense of what happened. As one seeks silence and the other demands answers, their friendship is tested by fear, guilt, and the search for justice.
gh63-104.editorial: A swimming pool and a girls' friendship together hold the silence after trauma. You'll like it if you value underwater photography, bodily sensation and keeping each other company.
gh63-104.contentNote: Content details have not yet been reviewed. This is not an assurance of no sensitive material or suitability for all ages.
gh63-104.bio: Fernanda Tovar trained in Mexico and joined Berlinale Talents. Documentary shorts preceded her first fiction feature, Sad Girlz.

gh63-105.title: A Family
gh63-105.syn: Teenagers Eli and Nina struggle to stay afloat as their parents' marriage dissolves into a bitter divorce. Forced to choose between their mother and father amid an escalating custody battle, the siblings retreat into their own worlds, drifting further apart in grief. Through their parallel journeys, they gradually discover that they are searching for the same things: love, recognition, and a place to belong.
